title: Happy Gilmore
logline: Adam Sandler as a failed hockey player with a 400-yard slapshot drive who joins the pro golf tour.
overview: Failed hockey player-turned-golf whiz Happy Gilmore — whose unconventional approach and antics on the green courts the ire of rival Shooter McGavin — is determined to win a PGA tournament so he can save his granny's house with the prize money. Meanwhile, an attractive tour publicist tries to soften Happy's image.
tagline: He doesn't play golf... he destroys it.

jokes.text: My mom didn't [worship hockey]. So she moved to Egypt, where there's not a hockey rink within 1500 miles.
jokes.setup: Happy says his dad worshipped hockey, his mom didn't — a mundane marital disagreement
jokes.punchline: Her solution was moving to a country geographically incompatible with hockey, presented as perfectly logical
jokes.explanation: The joke works because the extreme specificity (1500 miles, Egypt) makes the absurd logic feel like a real data point. Good economy — the punchline is delivered instantly after the setup with no wasted words.

jokes.text: She dressed like Gene Simmons from KISS to cheer me up. She's the sweetest person in the world.
jokes.setup: Happy is describing his grandmother trying to comfort him after his father's funeral
jokes.punchline: The comforting act was dressing like a KISS frontman — the incongruity of a sweet grandmother in full Gene Simmons makeup is the gag, made warmer by Happy's completely sincere endorsement
jokes.explanation: The joke has genuine warmth underneath the absurdity — Happy means every word, which makes it funnier. The specificity of Gene Simmons over any other rock star is good instinct. Establishes Grandma as a character immediately.

jokes.text: That kid stole my party blower. Instead of asking for it back, I hit him in the head repeatedly with a hammer.
jokes.setup: Happy is explaining he 'developed a short fuse' after his dad died — a sympathetic framing
jokes.punchline: The disproportionate violence (hammer, repeatedly) for a stolen party blower, delivered with complete matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's better jokes. The euphemistic framing ('short fuse') sets up a minor grievance, then the response is maximally disproportionate. 'Repeatedly' is the key word — doing it once might be an accident; doing it repeatedly is a character. Perfectly economical and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Most of the time, I was quick to say I was sorry.
jokes.setup: Happy just described beating a kid with a hammer over a party blower
jokes.punchline: 'Most of the time' implies this happened enough times that he has an average to report — the qualifier makes it worse
jokes.explanation: The 'most of the time' qualifier is doing enormous comedic work in four words — it implies a pattern, admits occasional non-apology, and maintains Happy's completely sincere self-image as a reasonable person. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: I still hold two league records: most time spent in the penalty box...and I was the only guy to ever try to stab someone with his skates.
jokes.setup: Happy proudly lists his junior hockey accomplishments
jokes.punchline: The second 'record' — not just being penalized a lot, but being uniquely violent in a way that required a first-ever rule — escalates perfectly from the first
jokes.explanation: The two-part structure is well-engineered: penalty box record is funny but expected; stabbing with skates is the genuine escalation. 'The only guy to ever try' (not succeed, but try) is the precise word choice that makes it funnier — it implies effort and intent.

jokes.text: I'm a good shot with a nail gun. But one day my boss, Mr. Larson, got in the way.
jokes.setup: Happy lists his various jobs; mentions being good with a nail gun
jokes.punchline: The boss 'got in the way' — implying Happy shot him with the nail gun, presented as a workplace accident rather than assault
jokes.explanation: Classic Happy deadpan violence framing. 'Got in the way' is the right euphemism — passive, blameless from Happy's perspective. Slightly less impactful than the hammer joke because it's a similar structure.

jokes.text: Apparently, he also has a short fuse. Look at the monster.
jokes.setup: Happy shot his boss with a nail gun; the boss is now presumably injured and furious
jokes.punchline: Happy diagnoses his boss with the same character flaw he has, completely lacking self-awareness, then calls him a 'monster' as if he's the innocent party
jokes.explanation: This is sharp character comedy — Happy's total lack of self-awareness is the engine of the whole film and this line crystallizes it perfectly. Calling the nail-gunned boss a 'monster' while narrating his own violence as reasonable is the purest expression of Happy's worldview. Strong character integration score justified.

jokes.text: He got in a few lucky punches, but I feel I won the fight.
jokes.setup: Happy's boss beat him up after being shot with a nail gun
jokes.punchline: Happy's subjective scoring of the fight ('I feel I won') after conceding the boss landed multiple hits — delusional self-assessment
jokes.explanation: Another beat of Happy's delusional self-image. Works well but is less surprising at this point in the montage — the character voice is established enough that this is confirmation rather than revelation.

jokes.text: Not a strong skater. Nor the best puck handler. But, my God... What a shot.
jokes.setup: Scouts are evaluating Happy — cataloguing his serious deficiencies as a hockey player
jokes.punchline: The reversal: despite being terrible at the actual skills of hockey, his shot is so extraordinary the scouts are awestruck — sets up the entire film's premise
jokes.explanation: Functional premise-establishing joke. The pause before 'What a shot' and the visual of the puck exploding the goal work together. More of a plot beat than a pure joke, but the comedic misdirection (cataloguing failures before the reversal) is competently done.

jokes.text: Coach, what's going on? What about me? / Gilmore. / I called your number, didn't I? / No, you didn't. / Well, better luck next year.
jokes.setup: Numbers are being called for the team; Happy is not among them
jokes.punchline: The coach's flat 'Well, better luck next year' after Happy correctly points out his number wasn't called — the coach simply doesn't care enough to even pretend
jokes.explanation: The coach's total indifference is the joke — he doesn't even try to manage Happy's feelings. Competent but not exceptional. The 'That wasn't very nice!' reaction from Happy that follows adds a beat.

jokes.text: That wasn't very nice! [Happy's reaction to being cut]
jokes.setup: Happy has just been dismissed by the coach with zero empathy
jokes.punchline: Happy's response — 'That wasn't very nice!' — is the complaint of a child, wildly understated given his rage throughout the montage
jokes.explanation: The unexpected gentleness of 'That wasn't very nice!' from someone who beat a child with a hammer and stabbed people with skates is the incongruity that makes it land. Good economy — four words do the work.

jokes.text: You think you're better than me?! [screamed at no one visible, in the parking lot]
jokes.setup: Happy leaves the tryout, furious
jokes.punchline: He screams 'You think you're better than me?!' apparently at a random person or at the world — the question implies he's picking a fight with an existence that has wronged him
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. The indiscriminate rage directed at an unclear target captures Happy's entire psychology. This line recurs throughout the film, earning a quotability boost.

jokes.text: Where you going? I got Subway. / I already ate. / I knew the guy working there, so we got extra meatballs.
jokes.setup: Happy's girlfriend is clearly leaving him; he tries to get her to stay
jokes.punchline: His pitch to save the relationship is Subway sandwiches with extra meatballs as a favor — completely tone-deaf to the gravity of the moment
jokes.explanation: Happy's obliviousness is the joke — the relationship is visibly collapsing and his response is to sell her on extra meatballs. The 'I knew the guy' detail adds a layer of Happy thinking this is a genuinely compelling offer.

jokes.text: I am good! You know what? You're a lousy kindergarten teacher! I saw the finger paintings you bring home — they suck!
jokes.setup: Terry tells Happy he'll never be a pro hockey player and he's going nowhere
jokes.punchline: Happy's comeback attacks her profession — but the insult is 'the finger paintings suck,' which reveals he has no better material than critiquing five-year-olds' artwork
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. The specificity of 'finger paintings suck' as a devastating insult is exactly right — Happy is trying to hurt her feelings with the best weapon he has, and the best he can do is criticize children's art. It reveals his immaturity while being completely believable as something he genuinely believes is a good burn.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean that. They're excellent finger paintings.
jokes.setup: Happy just savaged the finger paintings as his big insult
jokes.punchline: His immediate sincere retraction — specifically praising the paintings as 'excellent' — shows he actually feels bad about criticizing kindergarteners' art
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel. The apology escalates rather than defuses — Happy's moral conscience is activated not about destroying his relationship, not about screaming at his girlfriend, but specifically about having maligned five-year-olds' finger paintings. 'They're excellent finger paintings' delivered sincerely while she's walking out is comedy perfection. Exceptional character integration: only Happy would do this.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean that. I just yell 'cause I get so scared. Scared of being a nobody.
jokes.setup: Happy told his girlfriend to 'Get the hell out!' and 'Who needs you!'
jokes.punchline: His immediate pivot to vulnerable emotional honesty — 'I just yell 'cause I get so scared' — is a sudden gear-shift that is both pathetic and oddly sincere
jokes.explanation: More cringe than comedy here — the joke is the emotional whiplash, but it plays more as character development than a pure laugh line. Functional but not especially well-crafted as a joke.

jokes.text: Why don't you come back upstairs, honey? I'll give you the old snoochy-snoo kissy-wissy.
jokes.setup: Happy has gone from rage to vulnerability to now trying to seduce his departing girlfriend with baby talk
jokes.punchline: 'Snoochy-snoo kissy-wissy' — this large, violent, angry man's seduction vocabulary is nursery-level baby talk
jokes.explanation: The specific invented phrase 'snoochy-snoo kissy-wissy' is funny precisely because it's so infantile coming from this character. The incongruity between Happy's established violence and this tender baby-talk register is the whole joke, and it works.

jokes.text: Where are you taking her stuff? / I'm not taking her stuff, the government is. It's not like I'm taking her stuff over to my place.
jokes.setup: Happy is upset about his grandmother's belongings being seized
jokes.punchline: The agent's bureaucratic hair-splitting — 'I'm not taking her stuff, the government is' — followed by the defensive specificity of 'not like I'm taking it to my place,' which implies exactly that fear
jokes.explanation: The agent's pedantic distinction is a nice character detail — he's not a villain, just a bureaucrat protecting his professional identity. The 'not to my place' denial is a good specific detail that implies he's heard this accusation before.

jokes.text: But she's an old lady. Look at her. She's old. / You can't just take her stuff. She's too old.
jokes.setup: Happy is arguing against the repossession
jokes.punchline: Happy's entire legal argument is 'she's old' — repeated three times as if the repetition will make it more convincing, with 'look at her' as his evidentiary exhibit
jokes.explanation: Happy's argument deteriorating into 'she's too old' is good character comedy — he has no tools beyond loudness and repetition. Works because of his complete sincerity.

jokes.text: He hates me. [said to Grandma after the agent leaves]
jokes.setup: The IRS agent explicitly said 'No, I don't hate you'
jokes.punchline: Happy's immediate re-interpretation of 'I don't hate you' as evidence of hatred — a reaction beat of willful contrarianism
jokes.explanation: Three words that reveal Happy's paranoid victimhood perfectly. Good economy, modest originality — the 'he said he didn't but I know he does' beat is familiar but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Silver Acres Rest Home. It looks more like a country club. Nice grass, nice people. I hope you brought your bathing suit.
jokes.setup: Happy is depositing Grandma at what is clearly a dreary old folks' home
jokes.punchline: His absurdly positive spin — 'looks more like a country club,' 'bathing suit' — is either complete denial or an attempt to sell Grandma on the place, both of which are funny
jokes.explanation: Functional irony — the gap between Happy's sales pitch and the grim reality is the joke. Not especially memorable but serves the scene.

jokes.text: Get me out of here!!! [Grandma screaming as residents mob her]
jokes.setup: Happy has just told Grandma she'll 'make friends in no time'
jokes.punchline: Grandma is immediately swarmed by desperate residents and screams to escape — instant deflation of Happy's optimism
jokes.explanation: Quick visual payoff on Happy's optimism. The speed of the reversal (he literally just finished saying she'd make friends) is what makes it work. Slapstick visual with a good structural beat.

jokes.text: She got hit by a car. She's dead. [Happy answering Grandma's question about his girlfriend]
jokes.setup: Grandma sweetly asks how his 'nice girlfriend' is doing
jokes.punchline: Happy's completely flat 'She got hit by a car. She's dead.' — no emotion, no elaboration, immediately moving on to the tax problem
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy and delivery. Happy's compressed 'She got hit by a car. She's dead.' treats this as a minor administrative update before getting to the real topic (the taxes). The two-sentence construction — fact, then confirmation — is precisely right. The pivot to 'Listen, I will get that $270,000' is what seals it.

jokes.text: Nursing home orderly: 'Pardon me, but it's nap time.'
jokes.setup: An emotional farewell scene between Happy and Grandma
jokes.punchline: The orderly interrupts with cheerful mundane efficiency — nap time cannot be delayed for sentiment
jokes.explanation: Minor punctuation gag. The cheerful intrusion deflates the emotional moment. Standard sitcom beat, nothing exceptional. Happy's response ('Nap time — that sounds nice') adds a mild character touch.

jokes.text: Nap time — that sounds nice. [Happy says wistfully as he leaves the nursing home]
jokes.setup: An elderly resident announces it's nap time
jokes.punchline: Happy — a grown man who just had his world destroyed — genuinely envies the nap schedule
jokes.explanation: Small but warm joke — Happy's sincere 'that sounds nice' in the midst of his life crumbling is a good character beat. Modest craft but effective as a beat.

jokes.text: Buddy, do me a favor. You see that lady? She's very important to me. I want you to take extra special care of her. [slips money] / I can't accept that. But this is what I can do: I can take extra special care of that young lady for nothing.
jokes.setup: Happy tries to bribe the nursing home orderly to look after Grandma
jokes.punchline: The orderly self-righteously refuses the bribe, then offers the exact same service for free — making the refusal of the bribe completely pointless and slightly absurd
jokes.explanation: The orderly's principled stand that leads to the same outcome is a nice subversion. Foreshadows that this orderly is not what he seems (he will be revealed as abusive later in the film), giving the scene a rewatch dark quality.

jokes.text: You could trouble me for a warm glass of shut the hell up. / Go to sleep or I will put you to sleep. / Check out the name tag. You're in my world now, Grandma.
jokes.setup: An elderly resident sweetly asks the orderly for a warm glass of milk to help her sleep
jokes.punchline: 'A warm glass of shut the hell up' — a villain reveal disguised as a wordplay twist, followed by escalating menace
jokes.explanation: One of the great quotable lines from this film. 'Warm glass of shut the hell up' is structurally perfect — it mimics the rhythmic shape of the actual request ('warm glass of milk') and substitutes the impossible object. It's immediately followed by an escalation ('put you to sleep') and capped by the genuinely menacing 'You're in my world now, Grandma' with the name-tag detail. This is the rare joke that is also a perfect villain introduction. Approaches the craft anchor for 8+.

jokes.text: Bet you I can hit a ball past that tree. / Twenty bucks says you can't. / Morons, I told you I want to watch the hockey game. Cut the golf sissy crap and finish up.
jokes.setup: Construction workers are goofing around with a golf club on the job site
jokes.punchline: Happy's contemptuous 'golf sissy crap' — the man who is about to become a golf prodigy dismisses the sport with maximum disdain
jokes.explanation: The rewatch bonus is strong — knowing Happy's destiny makes 'golf sissy crap' funnier. As a first-watch joke, it's functional irony. The setup of the whole scene leading to his dismissal of golf works as premise irony.

jokes.text: Oh, you got a hold of that one! / You try it. / It's not as easy as it looks. / Sorry, ladies. I'm not the golfing type.
jokes.setup: Workers goad Happy into trying to hit a golf ball
jokes.punchline: 'Sorry, ladies. I'm not the golfing type.' — Happy's condescending dismissal right before he will hit it 400 yards
jokes.explanation: The 'sorry, ladies' condescension as Happy insults the game before accidentally mastering it is an effective setup for the reversal. The rewatch bonus applies — 'not the golfing type' takes on new meaning.

jokes.text: Look at this stupid thing. This will be hilarious. Look how he's standing. [Happy takes absurd hockey-style stance with golf club]
jokes.setup: Happy prepares to hit the golf ball; workers mock his bizarre stance
jokes.punchline: The visual of Happy's full-body hockey slapshot approach to a golf tee — the incongruity of athletic form borrowed from the wrong sport entirely
jokes.explanation: This is the film's core visual joke — the slapshot/golf swing hybrid — playing for the first time. The workers' mockery ('this will be hilarious') sets up the reversal perfectly. High impact because the visual of the running approach and full-body swing is genuinely funny physical comedy.

jokes.text: Holy shit. / That house is 400 yards away. / Is that good?
jokes.setup: Workers laughed at Happy's ridiculous swing form
jokes.punchline: The ball travels 400 yards; Happy's innocent 'Is that good?' — he has no frame of reference for golf excellence
jokes.explanation: The 'Is that good?' is the perfect cap to the reversal — Happy is the only person present who doesn't understand what just happened. High impact because this is the film's premise-establishing moment and the audience has been waiting for it.

jokes.text: You hit him! / He shouldn't have been standing there.
jokes.setup: Happy's prodigious drive apparently hit someone
jokes.punchline: Happy's instant deflection — 'He shouldn't have been standing there' — is complete victim-blaming delivered without a flicker of guilt
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback to Happy's established pattern of injuring people and blaming them for being in the way. 'He shouldn't have been standing there' in seven words establishes Happy's moral framework cleanly.

jokes.text: You made a bet. Pay the man. [Happy refusing to let someone weasel out of the $20 bet after a bystander gets hit]
jokes.setup: Happy hit a bystander; a worker tries to avoid paying the golf bet
jokes.punchline: Happy's priorities — someone is injured but Happy is focused on collecting his $20 — reveals his value system perfectly
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — the callousness about the injury is the joke, delivered through Happy's single-minded financial focus. Economical.

jokes.text: Thanks. Tell your friends. / Step right up, folks! See if you can outdrive the amazing Golf Ball, uh, Whacker Guy!
jokes.setup: Happy has just demonstrated his incredible drive; a worker turns it into a carnival attraction
jokes.punchline: 'The amazing Golf Ball, uh, Whacker Guy' — the worker can't come up with a golf term but commits fully to the showman bit anyway
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence search for the right word ('uh, Whacker Guy') is the comedic moment — the worker's enthusiasm is bigger than his vocabulary. Good pacing.

jokes.text: It's in the hips. Fifty bucks I can hit it over the highway.
jokes.setup: Happy is giving terrible golf advice to a worker while also hustling
jokes.punchline: His pivot from instructor to gambler — mid-lesson he immediately looks for a bigger bet — shows his entire character
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat — Happy's entrepreneurial instinct kicking in. 'It's in the hips' becomes a recurring bit (Chubbs will use it later), giving it callback value.

jokes.text: Just 364 more days till the next hockey tryouts. I got to get tough.
jokes.setup: Happy has been deliberately running into things to train for hockey
jokes.punchline: He's not training to be a golfer (his actual future); he's torturing himself for hockey tryouts a full year away — the specificity of '364 days' shows he's been counting
jokes.explanation: '364 more days' is the key detail — Happy has been counting since the rejection, he knows the exact number, and he is absolutely committed to a path that is clearly not his destiny. Pure character comedy with good economy.

jokes.text: So you're a hockey player. You got to give that up and concentrate on golf. / Who are you? / I'm the club pro here — Chubbs Peterson. I'm offering to teach you how to play golf, personally, for free. / No.
jokes.setup: A clearly knowledgeable golf professional makes Happy a generous offer
jokes.punchline: Happy's immediate flat 'No' — no consideration, no interest, no politeness
jokes.explanation: The monosyllabic 'No' after all of Chubbs's buildup is well-timed. Economy is perfect — Happy doesn't need a speech, just pure disinterest.

jokes.text: What happened? / I wasn't allowed to play pro anymore. / I'm sorry. Because you're black? / Hell, no. An alligator bit my hand off.
jokes.setup: Chubbs says Sports Illustrated said he'd be the next Arnold Palmer, then something prevented his pro career
jokes.punchline: Happy assumes racial discrimination (a reasonable real-world guess for 1965); the actual answer — alligator attack — is a completely unexpected escalation into absurdist territory
jokes.explanation: Exceptional misdirection. The setup guides the audience toward a serious, emotionally resonant answer (racial discrimination) — which would have been both true to history and dramatically heavy. The pivot to 'alligator bit my hand off' is a perfect tonal swerve. Happy's sincere guilt ('I'm sorry') at the wrong assumption makes the punchline land harder. 'Hell, no' as the rejection of the assumption is timed beautifully. This is the film's best pure joke-craft moment alongside the warm milk line.

jokes.text: Chubbs: 'Hell, no. An alligator bit my hand off.'
jokes.setup: Happy's racism guess; the audience expects a civil-rights-era sports story
jokes.punchline: 'An alligator bit my hand off' — delivered flatly as the actual reason
jokes.explanation: The punchline itself. 'Hell, no' (rejecting the racism guess) followed by the most unexpected possible alternative is perfect. Five words that completely redirect the scene. The economy is excellent, Chubbs's flat delivery presumably makes it land harder. Strong absurdist originality in the specific choice of 'alligator.'

jokes.text: But I tore one of that bastard's eyes out. Look at that. [Chubbs shows Happy a preserved alligator eye]
jokes.setup: Chubbs has described the alligator attack that ended his career
jokes.punchline: He carries the alligator's eye as a trophy — the escalation from victim to collector is the joke, delivered with complete pride
jokes.explanation: The eye-in-pocket detail is what elevates the alligator bit from a good joke to a great one. That Chubbs carries the eye at all times — as a trophy, as a warning — tells you everything about his character. The rewatch bonus is real: paying attention to the eye pays off massively at the film's climax.

jokes.text: Golf requires goofy pants and a fat ass. Talk to my neighbor — a great golfer. Huge ass.
jokes.setup: Chubbs argues golf requires talent and self-discipline like any sport
jokes.punchline: Happy's counter-argument reduces golf to wardrobe and body type — but the kicker is 'talk to my neighbor... huge ass,' which treats the neighbor as evidence in a legal argument
jokes.explanation: The punchline isn't the goofy pants observation (that's the setup) — it's 'huge ass' being cited as empirical evidence. Happy citing his neighbor as an expert witness to his ass-based golf theory is very good character comedy.

jokes.text: Get that gold jacket I never got. / Gold jacket, green jacket — who cares?
jokes.setup: Chubbs is emotionally invested in Happy winning the Tour Championship and its gold jacket
jokes.punchline: Happy, who knows nothing about golf, dismisses the gold jacket/green jacket distinction as meaningless — blaspheming golf's most sacred prize
jokes.explanation: Happy's dismissal of the Masters green jacket as equivalent to 'some other jacket' is excellent ignorance comedy. Rewatch bonus because the jacket becomes the film's central MacGuffin.

jokes.text: Don't worry. It's made of wood — real sturdy. [Chubbs offers Happy his prosthetic hand to shake; it falls off]
jokes.setup: Happy tries to shake Chubbs's hand; it appears to be a prosthetic
jokes.punchline: Chubbs reassures Happy ('real sturdy') right as the hand presumably detaches or malfunctions — the false confidence is the joke
jokes.explanation: The prosthetic hand gag is a solid physical comedy callback to the alligator revelation. 'Real sturdy' as it fails is the right ironic framing. The visual of the wooden hand is essential.

jokes.text: Hey, Chubbs... what kind of big bucks? [Happy, now fully turned around, suddenly very interested]
jokes.setup: Chubbs baited Happy with 'big bucks'
jokes.punchline: Happy's immediate reversal — now completely engaged — reveals that his entire resistance was performative; money was always the answer
jokes.explanation: The turnaround is well-executed — Happy has been making a principled stand against golf for the whole scene and immediately abandons it for money. The pause before 'Hey, Chubbs' is the comedic timing that makes it work.

jokes.text: Whoa — must be Burt Reynolds or something. [Happy sees an expensive car at the golf course]
jokes.setup: Happy arrives at the upscale golf course and sees a fancy car
jokes.punchline: His frame of reference for extreme wealth is 'Burt Reynolds' — a very Happy Gilmore-specific cultural referent
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — the specificity of Burt Reynolds as the pinnacle of wealth is a time-capsule detail that's charming but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: You going to recite me a poem? Geez, you love this golf stuff.
jokes.setup: Chubbs enthusiastically describes the beauty of the golf course (blue skies, fresh-cut grass, birds chirping)
jokes.punchline: Happy's contemptuous 'You going to recite me a poem?' reframes Chubbs's sincere joy as laughable sentimentality
jokes.explanation: The poem line is a good specific insult — 'poem' captures exactly the kind of sensitive appreciation Happy finds repugnant. Character-consistent.

jokes.text: A guy your size — why not play a real sport, like football? / My nana wouldn't let me. Said it was too dangerous. / Yeah, good call.
jokes.setup: Happy questions why a giant man plays golf instead of football
jokes.punchline: The giant man's nana protected him from football as 'too dangerous' — the irony that this enormous person was kept from a sport by a protective grandmother is punctured by Happy's dry 'Yeah, good call'
jokes.explanation: The 'nana' detail is the right specific word — not 'grandmother' or 'mom,' but 'nana,' which makes the giant seem genuinely sweet and obedient. 'Yeah, good call' is deadpan and well-timed.

jokes.text: Right now I'm working on a promotion — / You know what would be great? If I could get a Pepsi. / Sure. / Oh, miss? Diet.
jokes.setup: Virginia, the Tour's PR Director, is trying to pitch Happy on a promotional opportunity
jokes.punchline: Happy interrupts her mid-sentence to ask a passing attendant for a Pepsi — then amends it to Diet, completely derailing her pitch and treating her like she exists to get him drinks
jokes.explanation: Happy's obliviousness to Virginia's professional status and conversation is good character comedy. The 'Diet' amendment as an afterthought shows Happy's attention was entirely on the drink, not her pitch. Good cringe beat.

jokes.text: Hey, thanks for dressing up. / If I wore clothes like those, I'd have to kick my own ass.
jokes.setup: Shooter and Happy encounter each other; Shooter makes a mild dig at Happy's clothes
jokes.punchline: Happy's escalating comeback — he doesn't just defend himself, he implies he'd assault himself if he dressed that way
jokes.explanation: Happy's first real face-off with Shooter. 'I'd have to kick my own ass' is a good line — the self-referential violence threat, applied to Shooter's clothing, is consistent with Happy's worldview and quotable. Good intro to their rivalry.

jokes.text: Thank you, Doug. I saw Doug play yesterday. He spends more time in the sand than David Hasselhoff.
jokes.setup: Shooter thanks the Tour president Doug for the introduction
jokes.punchline: Shooter immediately roasts his host — 'more time in the sand than David Hasselhoff' — a Baywatch reference implying Doug is both a bad golfer and a beach-loitering TV character
jokes.explanation: The Hasselhoff reference is specific enough to work — it's not just 'spends time in the sand,' the beach-celebrity comparison adds a layer. Establishes Shooter as a crowd-pleasing villain who makes jokes at others' expense. Slightly dated but well-constructed.

jokes.text: Although only one will become my colleague... all of you are now my friends.
jokes.setup: Shooter is making a motivational speech to competitors before the tournament
jokes.punchline: The paradox — only one of you can join me, but we're all friends — reveals Shooter's performative warmth masking his competitive ruthlessness
jokes.explanation: Good villain character work — the hollow 'we're all friends' from someone who clearly views everyone as competition. More character establishment than pure joke.

jokes.text: Where you taking those clubs, punk?! / Mr. Gilmore, I'm your caddy.
jokes.setup: A young caddy approaches Happy with his clubs
jokes.punchline: Happy, who has never played in a tournament, doesn't know what a caddy is — his threat to the caddy is both aggressive and innocent
jokes.explanation: Quick joke — Happy's default aggression turned on a child carrying his clubs. 'Punk' is the right word choice — it's how Happy talks to everyone regardless of their actual threat level.

jokes.text: They're my grandfather's. They're pretty old. / What should I do then? / Why don't you just watch me and make sure I don't do anything stupid?
jokes.setup: Happy refuses to let the caddy carry his clubs
jokes.punchline: 'Make sure I don't do anything stupid' — the irony that Happy, the most chaos-prone person at the tournament, is appointing a child as his behavior monitor
jokes.explanation: The rewatch bonus is strong — knowing what 'stupid' looks like for Happy, the idea of a child keeping him in check is very funny. First-watch, it's good ironic foreshadowing.

jokes.text: Where were you that time, dipshit? [Happy to his caddy after a competitor's good shot]
jokes.setup: Lafferty hits a good drive; the caddy presumably watched without intervening
jokes.punchline: Happy blames his caddy for Lafferty's good shot — as if the caddy should have somehow prevented it — using 'dipshit' on a child
jokes.explanation: Callback to Happy's bizarre caddy instructions — he's holding the kid responsible for a competitor's shot. The logic is completely deranged and totally Happy.

jokes.text: Probably the best I'll hit all day. [Lafferty after a mediocre drive, as Happy is about to hit 400 yards]
jokes.setup: Lafferty hits what appears to be a decent but not extraordinary drive
jokes.punchline: His self-satisfaction right before Happy makes his shot look laughable is dramatic irony — he doesn't know what's coming
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — Lafferty's pride is immediately deflated by Happy. Functional but the joke is in the subsequent contrast, not in this line itself.

jokes.text: Damn it! / Time! / Relax. Do what we discussed. Don't look at the green. Hit the ball. There's no goalie anywhere to block it. Remember, it's all in the hip.
jokes.setup: Happy is struggling to tee off in a real tournament; Chubbs coaches him
jokes.punchline: Chubbs has to explain to Happy that there's no goalie — translating golf into hockey logic to reach him — revealing the depths of Happy's golf ignorance
jokes.explanation: 'There's no goalie anywhere to block it' is a great line — it acknowledges that Happy's mental model of sport involves goalies, and Chubbs has to work within that model. Pure character-specific coaching that couldn't happen with any other character.

jokes.text: It's all in the hips. All in the hips. / It's all in the hips. / Get off me! / Just easing the tension. Just easing the tension. / Well, ease it on someone else.
jokes.setup: Chubbs is coaching Happy on the hip motion needed for the golf swing
jokes.punchline: Chubbs grabs Happy's hips and grinds against him from behind to demonstrate; Happy objects; Chubbs's 'just easing the tension' is both a terrible explanation and a complete non-answer
jokes.explanation: The 'it's all in the hips' escalation from verbal instruction to physical demonstration is a good physical gag. 'Ease it on someone else' is a good comeback. The callback to the earlier 'in the hips' line gives it added resonance.

jokes.text: What the hell? [reaction to Happy's drive sailing 400 yards; crowd goes silent then reacts]
jokes.setup: Happy, after all the nervous preparation, finally unleashes his full running slapshot drive in a real tournament
jokes.punchline: The crowd's stunned reaction — 'What the hell?' — mirrors the construction workers' response, confirming this is genuinely extraordinary; the visual of the ball traveling impossibly far is the payoff
jokes.explanation: High impact because this is the film's premise moment in a real competitive context. The 'What the hell?' callback to the construction workers' reaction is satisfying structural repetition. The impact score is high because the audience is experiencing what the film has been building to.

jokes.text: Good. Now we just worry about putting. / Oh, yeah. Putting.
jokes.setup: Chubbs is relieved the drive worked perfectly
jokes.punchline: Happy's 'Oh, yeah. Putting.' — delivered as if he just remembered putting exists, suggesting he has no idea how to do it and has not thought about it at all
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal beat after the triumph of the drive — Happy's 'Oh, yeah. Putting.' suggests he genuinely forgot that getting to the green is only half the job. Good economy and timing.

jokes.text: Chubbs gives complex putting instructions; Happy: 'Whoa, you're confusing me. Just let me put the ball in the hole.'
jokes.setup: Chubbs is explaining putting technique (shoulders, arms, wrists)
jokes.punchline: Happy reduces the entire complexity of putting to 'just let me put the ball in the hole' — as though the difficulty is administrative rather than technical
jokes.explanation: Happy's simplification of a complex skill is good character comedy. He's not being sarcastic — he genuinely thinks the concept isn't the problem. The setup (Chubbs's technical instructions) makes the punchline land harder.

jokes.text: Gallery member: 'Is he kidding?' — reaction to Happy's putting attempts
jokes.setup: Happy is attempting to putt
jokes.punchline: His putting is so catastrophically bad that a gallery member questions if it's intentional
jokes.explanation: Minor reaction beat. Functional laugh, relies entirely on the visual of Happy's putting being catastrophic. The line itself is unremarkable but the gallery reaction format is a classic comedy device.

jokes.text: This is pathetic.
jokes.setup: Happy has apparently been putting for a very long time with no success
jokes.punchline: The blunt 'This is pathetic' — no elaboration, no sympathy, just categorical dismissal
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum economy — works as a punctuation mark on the extended putting sequence. Not a crafted joke on its own but serves as the capper for the visual gag.

jokes.text: Good shot. / It's about time. / True. I just couldn't get the ball in the hole. I wanted to, but I couldn't.
jokes.setup: Happy finally sinks the putt after what appears to be an absurd number of strokes
jokes.punchline: Happy's earnest explanation — 'I just couldn't get the ball in the hole. I wanted to, but I couldn't' — as if this insight is valuable analysis rather than a tautology
jokes.explanation: 'I wanted to, but I couldn't' as sports analysis is perfect circular tautology — Happy believes he's providing useful insight. The sincerity is what elevates it from generic dumb-guy line to a specifically Happy observation. Good closing beat for the reel.

jokes.text: He shoots, he scores! That was much easier than putting. I should try and do that every time.
jokes.setup: Happy has just gotten a hole-in-one on a par four by using a hockey-style slap shot drive rather than conventional golf technique.
jokes.punchline: He casually concludes that skipping putting entirely by holing out from the tee is simply the superior strategy — without irony.
jokes.explanation: Classic Happy Gilmore character comedy — his complete sincerity makes this land. Only a character this oblivious to golf's fundamentals could deliver this line straight-faced, and the internal logic is genuinely funny: yes, if you could always hole out from the tee, putting would be redundant. The character integration is high.

jokes.text: So could a golfer with an arm growing out of his ass.
jokes.setup: A tour official enthusiastically suggests Happy's long drive could draw big crowds.
jokes.punchline: Shooter coldly points out that any sufficiently grotesque freak show would draw crowds — implying Happy is merely a novelty, not a golfer.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The image is specific, grotesque, and perfectly economical — Shooter dismisses Happy's draw while simultaneously defining his own elitist character. 'Arm growing out of his ass' is vivid and unexpected enough to be genuinely funny, not just an insult. High originality, great economy, strong character voice. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Think of it this way. The other team has pulled their goalie. It's wide open. All you have to do is tap it in.
jokes.setup: Happy needs to sink a putt to qualify; the advisor tries to calm him down.
jokes.punchline: The advisor translates golf into hockey language ('other team pulled their goalie') to reach Happy's brain — a funny acknowledgment that Happy only understands sport through a hockey lens.
jokes.explanation: Smart character bit — it acknowledges Happy's one-track hockey mind and the other character's attempt to meet him there. Works as setup for the extended 'tap it in' sequence that follows.

jokes.text: All you have to do is tap it in. Just tap it in. Just tap it in. Give it a little tappy. Tap, tap, tap-a-roo.
jokes.setup: Happy has been told repeatedly to 'just tap it in' — a simple instruction for a short putt. He begins repeating the phrase to himself as a mantra while attempting the putt.
jokes.punchline: The repetition escalates into absurdist self-talk ('tap-a-roo'), culminating in him clearly missing the putt spectacularly despite the simplicity of the task.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most quotable sequences. The escalating self-talk — 'just tap it in... give it a little tappy... tap, tap, tap-a-roo' — is perfectly structured absurdism. Each iteration degrades slightly until 'tap-a-roo' which is delightfully stupid. The structure is tight: simple advice → mantra → childlike nonsense → failure. High quotability, strong character integration (only Happy talks to himself this way).

jokes.text: Grandma, Grandma... Grandma, Grandma.
jokes.setup: Happy has just choked catastrophically on what should have been a trivial putt, muttering increasingly childlike nonsense to himself.
jokes.punchline: In the wake of his failure, he calls out for his grandmother — a fully grown adult hockey player reverting to a child's comfort instinct in public.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-placed beat that deepens the 'tap it in' sequence. Happy's emotional regression to calling for Grandma after a public sporting failure is very on-brand and earns a solid laugh without needing more words.

jokes.text: I got a hockey record. I tried to stab someone with my skate. Nobody else ever did that.
jokes.setup: Virginia Venit congratulates Happy and mentions his hole-in-one on a par four might be a record.
jokes.punchline: Happy casually one-ups with his real claim to fame: an attempted assault with a skate blade, delivered as a point of pride.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Happy Gilmore character joke. The casualness with which he volunteers violent criminal behavior as a point of pride, in polite company, to a PR director, is a great comic beat. The specificity ('with my skate') makes it funnier than a generic violence boast. High character integration — this only works from Happy.

jokes.text: That's wonderful.
jokes.setup: Happy has just casually disclosed that his greatest achievement is an attempted stabbing with a skate.
jokes.punchline: Virginia's flat 'That's wonderful' — clearly not meaning it — is the straight-man beat that sells the absurdity of Happy's disclosure.
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man deadpan that completes joke #6. Economical and functional — two words do exactly what they need to. Not exceptional on its own but it's a well-executed reaction beat.

jokes.text: I am a bit bummed. I thought we got money for this.
jokes.setup: Happy has just qualified for the Pro Tour and everyone is celebrating. Virginia is telling him about the upcoming tournament.
jokes.punchline: Happy deflates the moment by revealing he thought the qualifier itself paid prize money — his entire motivation exposed as transactional and naive.
jokes.explanation: Solid character beat — Happy's uncouth fixation on money undermines what should be a triumphant moment. Works as characterization comedy.

jokes.text: And the guy who comes in last? $2,400. So no matter what, I'll get some money.
jokes.setup: Virginia mentions the winner of the next tournament takes home $216,000, implicitly motivating Happy to compete seriously.
jokes.punchline: Happy immediately focuses on the last-place prize as his floor guarantee — he has no illusion of winning but is relieved he can't be shut out financially.
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — the audience expects Happy to react to the $216K prize, but he pivots to the floor as his realistic target. Reveals character while getting a laugh. The logic is sound in Happy's world.

jokes.text: Some might call it luck. I like to call it... well, luck, I guess. So what?
jokes.setup: Bob Barker / his advisor tells Happy that a lot of his round was luck. Happy starts to rebut with false confidence...
jokes.punchline: ...then immediately concedes mid-sentence that yes, it was luck — but he's defiant about it anyway ('So what?').
jokes.explanation: Smart structure — the setup feints at a confident rebuttal, then the character catches himself and collapses, but adds defiance ('So what?') to save face. The self-correction mid-sentence is well-constructed and very Happy. Good laugh.

jokes.text: Don't be an asshole. Give me six months. I'll work with you every day.
jokes.setup: Happy's mentor begs him to stay and train rather than rushing onto the Pro Tour.
jokes.punchline: The blunt 'Don't be an asshole' as an opening to a sincere, heartfelt request is jarring and funny — mixing genuine coaching with casual profanity in a way that undercuts the earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh from the contrast of sincere plea with casual profanity. Functional but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: My fingers hurt. / Well, soon your back will hurt because you just got landscaping duty.
jokes.setup: An elderly resident complains that her fingers hurt from the quilting work.
jokes.punchline: The orderly punishes the complaint by assigning harder physical labor — landscaping — which is a darkly funny abuse of authority over elderly people who can't fight back.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy that works because the cruelty is so matter-of-fact. The orderly's logic (you complain about fingers, I'll give you something harder) is absurd and vaguely villainous, which is funny in a dark way.

jokes.text: Anyone else's fingers hurt? [silence] I didn't think so.
jokes.setup: After punishing the complaining resident with landscaping duty, the orderly surveys the room.
jokes.punchline: The implied terrified silence from the other elderly residents — and his satisfied 'I didn't think so' — is a tiny power-trip moment played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The comedic pause is the joke — a room of scared elderly people not daring to complain. The orderly's smug satisfaction is funny because he's treating a nursing home like a gulag. Economy is excellent; the silence does the heavy lifting.

jokes.text: Why do you make me act like that, huh?
jokes.setup: The orderly has just threatened and bullied elderly residents into silence.
jokes.punchline: He immediately shifts blame onto the residents — an abuser's classic deflection, delivered with apparent sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy beat — the immediate self-victimizing after bullying is a recognizable and funny psychological type, well-deployed. Short and economical.

jokes.text: Oh, thank God! I can't stand to live in this place another minute!
jokes.setup: Happy visits his grandmother and emotionally tells her he's on the Pro Tour and might win the house back. He assumes she's happy at the nursing home.
jokes.punchline: Grandma immediately shatters his assumption — she hates it there and has been suffering. The sudden emotional reversal undercuts Happy's triumphant moment.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirect — the audience has been led to believe Grandma is content (she seemed okay in the previous scene). The violent reversal ('I can't stand to live in this place another minute!') is funny precisely because it's so immediate and total.

jokes.text: I thought you liked it here. That orderly is nice. Don't you like him?
jokes.setup: Happy is blindsided by his grandmother's revelation that she hates the nursing home.
jokes.punchline: Happy sincerely vouches for the orderly the audience just watched bully elderly people — the dramatic irony is rich because viewers know the orderly is the villain.
jokes.explanation: Works as dramatic irony callback — the audience knows something Happy doesn't, which creates a satisfying extra laugh layer. Happy's naivety about the orderly who was just menacing old ladies is funny and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Let the kid fix it for you. Get the little twisty knobs. [Happy attempts to fix air conditioner, it falls out the window]
jokes.setup: Grandma complains the air conditioner is broken and it's too warm. Happy confidently moves to fix it.
jokes.punchline: Happy's repair attempt sends the AC unit crashing out the window — he makes the situation dramatically worse through sheer incompetence.
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy escalation — the fix-it premise inverts into catastrophe. Standard slapstick, competently executed but not especially original. The setup phrase 'get the little twisty knobs' is a small verbal highlight.

jokes.text: Mister! Mister! Get this off of me! / I'll be right down! / You know that 'Mister, mister' lady? I think I killed her.
jokes.setup: The AC unit has fallen from the window and apparently landed on an elderly resident below.
jokes.punchline: Happy Gilmore casually informs someone that he 'thinks he killed her' — delivered with the mild concern of someone who's misplaced their keys.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'I think I killed her' is the entire joke, and it's well-calibrated dark comedy. Happy's affect is totally flat — not horrified, just mildly noting a problem. The identification of the victim as 'that Mister, mister lady' is a perfect specificity that makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Norman spends more time in the sand than David Hasselhoff.
jokes.setup: Shooter McGavin is at a bar with fellow golfers, entertaining them with quips.
jokes.punchline: The Baywatch reference — Hasselhoff running on the beach — is used as a benchmarking joke to insult a rival's bunker play. It's a sharp pop-culture simile.
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-constructed joke. The golf-specific setup ('time in the sand' = bunker play) connects cleanly to a cultural image (Hasselhoff on the beach), and both meanings are activated simultaneously. Good economy and originality for a one-liner.

jokes.text: Come on, that was funny. / It was the first time I heard it.
jokes.setup: Shooter delivers his Hasselhoff joke and waits for a bigger reaction from the room.
jokes.punchline: A fellow golfer's dry 'it was the first time I heard it' implies Shooter has recycled this joke many times — the room is not impressed.
jokes.explanation: A quick layered beat: it simultaneously mocks Shooter and validates the Hasselhoff joke as being good enough to repeat, while deflating Shooter's ego. Well-structured and economical.

jokes.text: Anyone tapped the keg yet? I'll pump. I'm Happy Gilmore.
jokes.setup: Happy arrives at a bar gathering of pro golfers — an exclusive world where he is an outsider.
jokes.punchline: His opening gambit to introduce himself is to offer to pump the keg — aggressively blue-collar and oblivious to the upscale social environment.
jokes.explanation: Solid fish-out-of-water character moment. Happy's social approach is endearingly wrong for the setting. The non-sequitur self-introduction at the end ('I'm Happy Gilmore') is a nice throwaway.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah? What's that? / Only the biggest tournament of the year. / Oh, really? Where's yours?
jokes.setup: Mark Lye mentions the Tour Championship jacket that the winner receives. Happy asks about it, is told it's the biggest tournament of the year.
jokes.punchline: Happy immediately asks where Mark's jacket is — implying Mark hasn't won it — without knowing if that's true. It's an accidental/instinctive diss.
jokes.explanation: Very economical burn — four words ('where's yours?') deliver a confident trash-talk that the whole bar reacts to. The fact that Happy probably didn't even intend it as a devastating insult makes it funnier. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Not if I have anything to do with it.
jokes.setup: Mark Lye says Shooter will have his jacket in three months. Shooter is standing right there.
jokes.punchline: Shooter responds to the third-person compliment about himself with an in-character competitive declaration — the self-aggrandizement is so automatic it's funny.
jokes.explanation: Minor Shooter character beat. Mildly funny but not especially crafted — it's the kind of line that fills space rather than earns a laugh.

jokes.text: Public relations lady, you seen Shooter McGavin? I need to beat the piss out of him.
jokes.setup: Happy has been tricked by Shooter into waiting on the ninth green at night. He finds Virginia Venit.
jokes.punchline: Happy announces his intention to assault Shooter to a PR professional — the person least likely to be a good confidant for this plan — as casually as if asking for directions.
jokes.explanation: Classic Happy obliviousness — volunteering violent plans to an authority figure. 'Beat the piss out of him' is colorfully physical. Works as characterization.

jokes.text: Let me guess -- the ninth green at nine trick. / It would appear so. / He does deserve a beating.
jokes.setup: Happy explains he was stood up on the ninth green. Virginia immediately deduces Shooter's trick.
jokes.punchline: Virginia — the PR Director — concedes that Shooter 'does deserve a beating,' which completely validates Happy's violent impulse before walking it back.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion — the authority character (PR Director) briefly agrees with the violent plan before thinking better of it. The deadpan 'he does deserve a beating' from someone who should be preventing beatings is a solid laugh.

jokes.text: My girlfriend's dead. She fell off a cliff and died on impact.
jokes.setup: Virginia and Happy are having a mild flirtatious conversation. She's being sympathetic. Happy apparently wants to explain his availability/emotional state.
jokes.punchline: Happy drops this devastating biographical fact with no emotional preamble — the specificity ('fell off a cliff... died on impact') delivered flatly is both dark and weirdly funny.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the delivery and context — the specificity ('died on impact') sounds like Happy is reading from a police report. It's dark, socially inappropriate, and very Happy. Functions as both tragedy and awkward-comedy.

jokes.text: Really? I'm sorry to hear that.
jokes.setup: Happy has just flatly announced his girlfriend's death as if commenting on the weather.
jokes.punchline: Virginia's entirely normal, slightly stunned 'Really? I'm sorry to hear that' plays perfectly against the absurdity of how Happy delivered it — the straight-man response sells the joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional straight-man beat that completes joke #26. Virginia's normalcy is the contrast the joke needs. Not funny on its own, but correctly placed.

jokes.text: Thanks, man. Here's my last buck. This is the last time. [Gambler begging at tournament]
jokes.setup: A crowd shot at the AT&T Invitational shows a fan desperately giving what appears to be his last dollar, muttering 'this is the last time.'
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of a golf tournament — an upscale sport — with a degenerate gambler's rock-bottom moment. The specificity of 'last buck' and 'last time' (delivered in a way that suggests it is definitely not the last time) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Background gag that works as color. The 'this is the last time' self-delusion of an addict is a recognizable type. Functional rather than crafted — it's atmosphere more than a joke.

jokes.text: Must be something in the water. Well, time to play golf.
jokes.setup: Shooter has been asked if he likes Portland and says every time he visits it's harder to leave. The interviewer probes this sentiment.
jokes.punchline: He nonsensically attributes Portland's charm to the water, then immediately cuts off the moment of apparent vulnerability with 'Well, time to play golf' — a total non-sequitur emotional shutdown.
jokes.explanation: Minor Shooter character bit — the swift pivot away from emotion into professionalism ('time to play golf') is a slight gag revealing his emotional vacuity. Competent filler.

jokes.text: I'm a hockey player playing golf today.
jokes.setup: Happy is being introduced before teeing off in his first Pro Tour event. He's apparently asked or stating something about himself.
jokes.punchline: He introduces himself by clarifying his primary identity — he's not a golfer, he's a hockey player who happens to be doing this — which is delightfully literal and self-aware.
jokes.explanation: Very economical character statement. Happy's self-identification as a hockey player mid-golf event is funny in its honesty and specificity. The comma-less directness ('playing golf today') makes it sound almost accidental.

jokes.text: On the Pro Tour, you provide your own [caddy]. / Really? [looks around, grabs random spectator]
jokes.setup: Happy is told he needs to supply his own caddy for the Pro Tour, something he didn't know.
jokes.punchline: Happy's immediate solution is to grab a random person from the crowd — treating a spectator as an ad-hoc employee.
jokes.explanation: Good physical problem-solving comedy — Happy's resourcefulness is both practical (in Happy's world) and absurd (in the real world). The randomness of the solution is the joke.

jokes.text: Easy with those clubs. They're antiques.
jokes.setup: Happy's randomly-grabbed spectator-turned-caddy handles Happy's golf bag.
jokes.punchline: Happy's golf clubs — clearly not professional equipment — being described as 'antiques' (precious, valuable) by Happy is a small character-consistent joke about his self-delusion.
jokes.explanation: Quick throwaway that works because it's so casually self-important. Happy's crummy clubs being treated like heirlooms is funny and consistent with his character.

jokes.text: I feel a lot of solid energy coming out of you. Good positive aura.
jokes.setup: Happy is introduced to Gary Potter, another golfer, on the first tee of his debut.
jokes.punchline: Gary immediately launches into new-age energy-aura talk with complete sincerity — his entire character is established in one sentence as a golf-world absurdist.
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment comedy — Gary Potter is the tour's mystic, introduced efficiently. The 'solid energy... positive aura' combination is a nicely specific new-age vocabulary.

jokes.text: Feel the flow, Happy. It's circular. It's like a carousel. You get on the horse. It goes up, down and around. Circular. Circle. With the music, the flow. All good things.
jokes.setup: Gary Potter continues dispensing new-age golf wisdom to Happy before his first tournament shot.
jokes.punchline: The 'advice' becomes increasingly free-associative and meaningless — carousel, horse, up down around, circular, circle, music — until it's pure sound that means nothing.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier extended character bits in the reel. The escalating meaninglessness of Gary's advice is well-constructed — it starts with something that sounds vaguely coherent ('circular energy') and degrades into pure word-salad ('circular. circle.'). The rhythm and repetition are essential to why it works.

jokes.text: Psycho. [after Gary Potter's carousel speech]
jokes.setup: Gary Potter has just delivered a lengthy, incoherent speech about carousels, circles, and energy.
jokes.punchline: Happy's one-word verdict — 'Psycho' — is the only appropriate response and lands as the capper to the whole absurdist monologue.
jokes.explanation: Perfect capper line. Maximum economy — one word dismantles a paragraph of nonsense. The reuse of 'Psycho' (which reappears later at 36:28) starts to become a running gag. 10/10 on economy because there is literally no more efficient way to deliver this joke.

jokes.text: Fu--, sh--, fu--, ass-- [Happy's running approach to the tee, cursing repeatedly]
jokes.setup: Happy prepares to take his first Pro Tour shot. The camera has been building the moment solemnly.
jokes.punchline: Happy's pre-shot routine is a running start accompanied by a stream of bleeping profanity — a hockey slap-shot approach on a golf course, treating the tee shot like a penalty shot.
jokes.explanation: Visually the most distinctively Happy moment in the reel — the full running-start, bleep-strewn approach to a golf shot is the film's core comedic premise made physical. High character integration because this is literally only possible from this character. The bleeping adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: Sorry. [after a massive drive lands in someone's gallery/yard]
jokes.setup: Happy's enormous drive has clearly gone somewhere unintended — possibly into the crowd or property adjacent to the course.
jokes.punchline: Happy's completely casual 'Sorry' — delivered with the affect of someone who bumped into you at a grocery store — is hilariously understated for the chaos he's apparently caused.
jokes.explanation: One-word joke that works through contrast — massive destruction, tiny response. Good economy. The character integration is decent because Happy's social calibration is always slightly off.

jokes.text: Psycho. [Gary Potter, watching Happy's shot]
jokes.setup: Gary Potter, the new-age mystic who lectured Happy about circular energy and carousels, watches Happy's chaotic running-start drive.
jokes.punchline: Gary uses Happy's own word back — 'Psycho' — the same word Happy used to describe him. The irony of the circular-energy guru calling someone else a psycho is the joke.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best constructed jokes in the reel. Gary Potter — who was just labeled 'Psycho' by Happy for his absurdist carousel speech — watches Happy sprint and swear through a golf shot and returns the exact same verdict. The symmetry is perfect, the economy is perfect, and the character irony (the mystic calling someone else crazy) is rich. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: What a shot by Happy Gilmore! / Who the hell is Happy Gilmore?
jokes.setup: Happy's debut drive is spectacular. Verne Lundquist calls it enthusiastically.
jokes.punchline: His broadcast partner Jack Beard reveals he has no idea who this person is — the anonymous newcomer whose shot just shocked everyone.
jokes.explanation: Classic sportscaster comedy — the enthusiastic call immediately deflated by the partner's obliviousness. The 'who the hell' adds the right amount of frustration to make it funnier than a plain 'who is Happy Gilmore?'

jokes.text: Oh, yeah! I got it! Like that, baby? Plenty more where that came from!
jokes.setup: Happy has apparently made another great shot and is celebrating on the course in front of a gallery.
jokes.punchline: His celebration is way over-the-top for golf — trash talk, chest-puffing, addressing the crowd like a hockey fighter — completely out of place in the genteel golf environment.
jokes.explanation: Fish-out-of-water physical comedy. The hockey-style celebration in golf is the film's central comic engine, well-executed here. Character integration is high but the specific lines aren't crafted — they're generic sports trash talk applied in the wrong context.

jokes.text: Five iron, huh? You're fired. Bye-bye.
jokes.setup: Happy's randomly-grabbed spectator-turned-caddy recommends a five iron for a shot. Happy disagrees, asks for his wedge, the caddy argues for a five iron.
jokes.punchline: After apparently hitting a great shot with his wedge, Happy fires his caddy on the spot with the casual finality of 'Bye-bye' — a dismissal no professional golfer would ever make mid-round.
jokes.explanation: Good setup-punchline with strong character integration — Happy's impulsive management style (firing someone who was just proven wrong with a breezy 'Bye-bye') is very consistent with his character. The 'Bye-bye' specifically is a great word choice — not 'you're fired, get out' but dismissive and casual.

jokes.text: What are you doing, Happy — riding a bull? You're acting like a damn fool!
jokes.setup: Happy is celebrating a good shot with his over-the-top hockey-style dance on the golf course.
jokes.punchline: His mentor compares the celebration to bull riding — an image specific enough to be funny — before the broader 'damn fool' verdict.
jokes.explanation: Solid reactive joke. The bull-riding image is vivid and specific — it paints exactly the kind of unhinged physical performance Happy is apparently doing. Sets up the 'bull dance' callback.

jokes.text: Doing the bull dance. Feeling the flow. Working it.
jokes.setup: Chubbs has just asked what Happy is doing — 'riding a bull?' Happy responds.
jokes.punchline: Happy sincerely adopts the bull-dance framing and adds his own phrase soup — 'feeling the flow. Working it.' — which also callbacks Gary Potter's 'feel the flow' language from earlier.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film and this reel's highest quotability. 'Doing the bull dance. Feeling the flow. Working it.' is a triple-phrase rhythm that works as both a callback to two previous jokes and a standalone absurdist declaration. The confidence and specificity of 'the bull dance' (treating a thrown-together name as an established thing) is perfect Happy Gilmore character. Extreme economy — nine words do enormous comedic work. Quotability is 9.5 because this line became a cultural reference. Justifies 8+ across the board.

jokes.text: His crowd seems unusually small for this type of moment. / Most people are over watching Happy Gilmore.
jokes.setup: The announcers cut to Shooter McGavin putting for the win on 18 — normally the climactic moment of a tournament.
jokes.punchline: The crowd is tiny because everyone has migrated to watch Happy Gilmore's chaos on another hole. Shooter's ceremonial victory is being ignored.
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — the juxtaposition of Shooter's empty victory ceremony with the crowd watching Happy underscores the central theme economically. Shooter's humiliation is the joke, delivered through the announcers with appropriate understatement.

jokes.text: Son of a bitch ball! Why didn't you go home?!
jokes.setup: Gary Potter has told Happy to 'send the ball home' as a putting visualization technique. Happy has apparently tried this and missed the putt.
jokes.punchline: Happy screams at the ball directly — treating it as a sentient disobedient entity — using Gary Potter's 'home' metaphor but with furious profanity instead of serene new-age calm.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that inverts Gary Potter's serene advice into furious confrontation. Happy has absorbed the metaphor but applied it with his actual personality — rage instead of serenity. The escalation from 'send him home' to 'son of a bitch ball!' is a sharp inversion.

jokes.text: That's your home! Are you too good for your home?! Answer me!
jokes.setup: Happy has already yelled at the ball for not going in. He continues the confrontation.
jokes.punchline: The escalation into 'are you too good for your home?!' treats the ball's failure to drop as a class-based insult — the ball is being snobby — which is completely unhinged and very funny.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the film. 'Are you too good for your home?!' is funny because it applies genuine class-based resentment logic to an inanimate object — the ball is being accused of thinking it's better than a golf hole. The 'Answer me!' at the end escalates to pure derangement. High character integration — Happy's working-class chip-on-shoulder being applied to golf equipment is perfect. Justifies 8+ score.

jokes.text: Suck my white ass, ball!
jokes.setup: Happy has been screaming at a golf ball that won't go in the hole, treating it as a defiant entity.
jokes.punchline: The final escalation of the ball-screaming sequence reaches its peak absurdity — Happy issues a graphic personal insult to a piece of sporting equipment.
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the three-beat ball-screaming escalation. The specificity ('white ass') is funnier than a generic profanity — it's weirdly specific and intensely personal for an inanimate target. Well-structured as the capper of the escalating sequence.

jokes.text: Draft a press release stating Gilmore is being thrown off the Tour. I want to see it by 6:00 p.m.
jokes.setup: Happy has just screamed profanity at a golf ball on live television at the Pro Tour.
jokes.punchline: The Commissioner's bureaucratic, process-oriented response to pure chaos — 'draft a press release... by 6 p.m.' — treats Happy's breakdown as an administrative problem.
jokes.explanation: Functional institutional-comedy beat — the bureaucratic deadpan response to chaos is a reliable joke type. Competent but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: I didn't see him play. I was too busy winning. But a 450-yard drive is impressive. / Yeah. Where did he finish again? Dead last? Yeah, he had a good day.
jokes.setup: Reporters ask Shooter about Happy Gilmore's debut. Shooter feigns disinterest before the pivot.
jokes.punchline: Shooter's mock-generous 'impressive' praise immediately inverted by 'where did he finish? Dead last? Yeah, he had a good day' — a masterclass in passive-aggressive sports media fake praise.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Shooter character moment — his ability to deliver a compliment and total dismissal in the same breath is exactly what makes him a great villain-comic character. 'Yeah, he had a good day' dripping with contempt after establishing Dead Last is a perfectly landed ironic button. Character integration is high — this is Shooter's specific voice.

jokes.text: Did he really make a 450-yard ace? Where's my check? We mail them next week. I want mine now. I don't have any checks. He got one. Give me one of them big ones, I don't care.
jokes.setup: Post-tournament, Happy is being interviewed. He hears about his own 450-yard ace (now growing in legend). Then pivots to demanding his check.
jokes.punchline: Happy's negotiating strategy for his prize money: 'He got one. Give me one of them big ones, I don't care.' — pointing at someone else's oversized novelty check as his target.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Happy's obliviousness to process (not understanding prize checks aren't handed out immediately) paired with his laser focus on 'one of them big ones' is funny. The specificity of 'I don't care' — meaning he wants the symbolic oversized check, not necessarily money — lands well.

jokes.text: Give me a beer, pal. Put that on my tab.
jokes.setup: Happy is at the prize money table after finishing dead last in his first tournament. He's being told about how checks are mailed.
jokes.punchline: Happy, having just finished last in a golf tournament, immediately orders a beer and runs a tab — treating his dead-last finish as a reason to celebrate or at minimum to drink.
jokes.explanation: Minor character beat. Functional but not especially crafted — running a tab at the event is a small Happy-consistent moment without a strong punchline.

jokes.text: I know what you're doing right now... and I don't like it. So just shut your trap before I put my foot in it.
jokes.setup: A golfer is suggesting to Happy that he'd be better suited for a long-drive contest or hustling at driving ranges rather than the Pro Tour.
jokes.punchline: Happy's response shows he's smarter than he looks (he correctly reads the condescension) but then threatens to put his foot in someone's 'trap' — which is funny because 'trap' means mouth but also sounds like a golf bunker.
jokes.explanation: Good beat that shows Happy's social intelligence is higher than expected — he reads the subtext correctly. The 'shut your trap before I put my foot in it' threat is an appropriately colorful Gilmore line.

jokes.text: I was on this tour for one reason — money. Now I got a new one — kicking your ass.
jokes.setup: Shooter has been condescending to Happy, calling him a freak, implying he's just a novelty who doesn't belong.
jokes.punchline: Happy upgrades his motivation from financial to personal vendetta — a crisp, funny declaration that the tour has become about Shooter specifically.
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-structured declaration — the pivot from money to 'kicking your ass' is sharp and economical. Good character voice and a quotable structure ('I was here for X, now I'm here for Y').

jokes.text: Let's do it. / I meant at golf.
jokes.setup: Happy threatens to kick Shooter's ass. Shooter accepts the challenge. Happy apparently moves toward him physically.
jokes.punchline: Shooter immediately clarifies 'I meant at golf' — he was issuing a sporting challenge, not a brawl invitation — the clarification itself is funny because it reveals Shooter's bravado doesn't extend to actual fighting.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — Shooter's big dramatic 'Let's do it' acceptance immediately deflated by his own clarification. The clarification is funnier because Shooter delivers it, not Happy — Shooter undercuts his own intimidating persona. Good character integration and very economical.

jokes.text: Just stay out of my way. Or you'll pay. Listen to what I say.
jokes.setup: Shooter is making his dramatic exit from the confrontation.
jokes.punchline: He accidentally — or deliberately — speaks in rhyme ('way / pay / say'), which is so unexpectedly goofy it derails his attempt at being threatening.
jokes.explanation: Very funny moment — the unintentional (or committed) rhyme scheme from a man trying to be menacing is a great character-comedy twist. It makes Shooter simultaneously threatening and ridiculous, which is exactly the right tone for the character.

jokes.text: Why don't I go eat some hay? I could make things out of clay and lay by the bay. What do you say?
jokes.setup: Shooter has accidentally rhymed his threat. Happy notices and responds in kind.
jokes.punchline: Happy commits fully to extending the rhyme scheme into pure nonsense — 'eat some hay... clay... lay by the bay... what do you say?' — turning Shooter's intimidation attempt into a collaborative nonsense poem.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel and a strong candidate for the best in the film. Happy's response is not just a comeback — it's a commitment to pure absurdist escalation. The genius is that his hay/clay/bay rhymes are COMPLETELY meaningless (eating hay, making things out of clay) which makes it even funnier than if he'd said something clever. It's the confidence of the commitment that makes it land. 'What do you say?' as the capper inverts Shooter's intimidation into a jovial invitation. This earns 8+ on originality because the specific choice of meaningless rhymes is what makes it exceptional — a lesser writer would have put a clever insult in there. Fully justified.

jokes.text: Hey, um... you want to get some food? / No, thanks. I don't date golfers. / Good. I'm a hockey player.
jokes.setup: Happy awkwardly attempts to ask Virginia Venit on a date after a tense negotiation about his behavior.
jokes.punchline: She deflects with 'I don't date golfers' — Happy immediately seizes on the technical loophole: he identifies as a hockey player, not a golfer, so the objection doesn't apply.
jokes.explanation: One of the best structured exchanges in the reel. The setup-punchline-counter-punchline is perfectly economical: she uses a rule to reject him, he finds a loophole in the rule using his established identity. 'Good. I'm a hockey player.' is a perfect button — it's both a callback to the film's premise and a genuinely clever romantic gambit. The confidence of the delivery is essential. Justifies 8+ across structure, character integration, and economy.

jokes.text: Happy Gilmore! Drive it 400 yards! / I can't believe I have fans. I waited all my life for that.
jokes.setup: Happy is approaching the tee at a new tournament and is suddenly greeted by fans who know who he is.
jokes.punchline: Happy's genuine emotional response — stunned disbelief that he has fans, expressed with the earnestness of someone who truly never expected public appreciation — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Sweet character moment — Happy's sincerity about having fans is funny because it's so unexpectedly vulnerable and honest. 'I waited all my life for that' from someone who stumbled into golf two weeks ago is a small irony.

jokes.text: How's that, uh, thing feeling? / Terrific. The mall comes out next week. / Well, you hardly even notice it.
jokes.setup: Happy greets an older man (Mr. Larson) who apparently has some kind of medical device or cast (a 'mall' — presumably a metal rod/hardware).
jokes.punchline: Happy's diplomatic 'you hardly even notice it' clearly applies to something very noticeable — the comedy is in Happy's social grace being completely inadequate but offered with sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Minor dark-comedy bit about medical hardware. Happy's attempt at social grace ('you hardly even notice it') is deadpan polite-lying humor. Works but isn't particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Trying to reach the green from here? That's not possible, sir. / I beg to differ. / Happy Gilmore accomplished that feat no more than an hour ago. / Well, moron, good for Happy— Oh, my God!
jokes.setup: A golfer dismisses the idea of reaching the green from an extreme distance as impossible, with an arrogant condescension.
jokes.punchline: His caddy points out Happy did exactly that, which the golfer dismisses with 'Well, moron, good for Happy—' mid-sentence before his own ball apparently accomplishes the same feat, cutting him off with 'Oh, my God!'
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured joke — the arrogant dismissal interrupted by its own refutation is a perfect irony structure. The 'Well, moron' aimed at the person who was right is an extra layer of hubris that makes the fall funnier. The mid-sentence 'Oh, my God!' cutoff is timed well.

jokes.text: Hey, Shooter, you forgot your nine iron. [Happy throws a golf club at Shooter]
jokes.setup: Happy spots Shooter McGavin on the course after their earlier confrontation.
jokes.punchline: Under the guise of helpfully returning a club, Happy hurls a nine iron at Shooter — a friendly action performed as projectile assault.
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy with a good structure — the polite pretext ('you forgot your nine iron') followed by an aggressive physical act. Happy's plausible deniability is non-existent and that's the joke. Well-integrated with his character.

jokes.text: It's the tour sensation, Happy Gilmore, who's attracting all types to this course. I even saw one guy wearing one of those beer-dispensing helmets.
jokes.setup: Announcer Verne Lundquist notes that Happy is drawing an unusually diverse crowd.
jokes.punchline: His specific example of the new crowd demographic — a beer-helmet guy — is a vivid image that captures the class distinction between traditional golf crowds and Happy's fanbase.
jokes.explanation: Good observational/class-comedy bit. The beer helmet is a specific, vivid image that efficiently communicates the social disruption Happy is causing in the golf world.

jokes.text: Damn you people. Go back to your shanties.
jokes.setup: Happy's rowdy, blue-collar fanbase is apparently disrupting the golf course — cheering, drinking, etc.
jokes.punchline: Shooter's furious 'go back to your shanties' perfectly captures his elitist contempt for the new crowd Happy has attracted — he's genuinely horrified that the wrong class of people is at his tournament.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Shooter line. 'Go back to your shanties' is specific, class-based, and deeply revealing of Shooter's character — he's not just annoyed by noise, he's offended by the demographic. High character integration and quotability. The specific word 'shanties' is a great choice over something generic like 'go home.'

jokes.text: What do you think? Slightly downhill? And slanting left. / No, you think that 'cause you only got one shoe on.
